top_comments.text:
1. What are the most common mistakes people make when using you incorrectly? Give me a comprehensive list so I know how to become a power user. (Run this prompt). 

2. I want you to take note of these mistakes and going forward I want you to tell me across all past, current, and future conversations. (Run that).

3. Every time I make one of those mistakes, I want you to coach me on how to be a better prompt engineer. (Run this prompt last).

top_comments.author: @CarsonBoyd
top_comments.text:
Here are the results of running the first prompt, in case you find it helpful.

Here's a comprehensive breakdown — organized by category, from most common to most costly:

---

## THE MOST COMMON CLAUDE MISTAKES

### 1. VAGUE OPENING PROMPTS
The single biggest one. "Write me a song about loss" gives me nothing to work with. No role, no tone, no target, no constraints. The more specific your opener, the better my first draft — and the less revision you need.

**Fix:** Role + goal + constraints + format in one prompt.

---

### 2. ACCEPTING DRAFT 1
Most people treat my first output as the answer. It's not — it's the starting point. I'm calibrating to you. The iteration loop is where quality actually happens.

**Fix:** Ask "Where is this weak?" or "What's missing?" before you lock anything.

---

### 3. STACKING MULTIPLE ASKS
"Write the chorus, suggest a title, give me Suno tags, and draft the YouTube description." Each ask competes for my attention and dilutes all of them.

**Fix:** One focused pass at a time. Get the chorus right, then move.

---

### 4. NOT GIVING ME A ROLE
"You" without a persona gets generalist output. "You are a veteran co-writer who values emotional directness and hates lyric clichés" gets a collaborator who thinks like one.

**Fix:** Assign a role at the start of any session that has a specific domain.

---

### 5. NOT SPECIFYING FORMAT
I'll default to whatever format feels natural to me. If you want prose, not bullets — say so. If you want three options, not one — say so. If you want no preamble — say so.

**Fix:** Always include format in your prompt. "No preamble. Start with the first line."

---

### 6. DROPPING CONTEXT BETWEEN SESSIONS
I remember nothing between conversations unless it's in your memory system. Starting a new session without re-establishing context means I'm flying blind.

**Fix:** End important sessions with a context capsule you can paste next time — "Here's where we are and what we need next."

---

### 7. NOT TELLING ME WHAT TO PRESERVE
"Revise this" with no constraints means I might improve one thing by breaking another. Sacred elements need to be declared.

**Fix:** "Keep [X] exactly. Change only [Y]."

---

### 8. TREATING MY QUESTIONS AS OPTIONAL
When I ask a clarifying question, it's because the answer will meaningfully change my output. Skipping it means I'll guess — and guessing costs revision time.

**Fix:** Answer my questions, or tell me to make a named assumption and proceed.

---

### 9. NEVER ASKING ME TO CRITIQUE MY OWN WORK
People use me to create but rarely to evaluate. I can tell you where a lyric stumbles, where an argument is weak, or what a skeptical reader would object to.

**Fix:** "What are the three weakest things about this?" after any draft.

---

### 10. SINGLE-TURN THINKING
Treating me like a search engine — one prompt, one answer, done. The real power is in multi-turn dialogue where you direct, I draft, you redirect, I refine.

**Fix:** Think of conversations as sculpting sessions, not vending machine transactions.

---

### 11. UNDER-SPECIFYING TONE
"Make it emotional" and "Make it urgent" and "Make it warm" are three different things. Vague tone notes get averaged output.

**Fix:** Use concrete anchors. Name a feeling, a texture, a reference artist, a scene.

---

### 12. NOT USING PERSONAS / SKILL FILES
General Claude is good. Loaded-skill Claude is a specialist. Most people never tell me to behave like a specific expert or load a relevant skill framework.

**Fix:** "You are a [specific expert]. Stay in that role for this conversation."

---

### 13. ASKING FOR TOO MUCH LENGTH BY DEFAULT
Longer isn't better. I'll pad if you don't constrain me. Constraints force clarity.

**Fix:** Set a word or line limit. "Max 50 words." "One verse only."

---

### 14. NOT USING THE DUAL-VOICE TEST
When you're stuck between directions, ask me for two radically different versions. Seeing the contrast often clarifies which direction is right faster than any discussion.

**Fix:** "Give me two versions — one [X], one [Y]. Make them genuinely different."

---

### 15. NEVER ASKING WHAT I'M ASSUMING
I fill gaps with assumptions. Those assumptions might be wrong. You won't know unless you ask.

**Fix:** "What are you assuming here?" after any complex output.

---

### QUICK REFERENCE — POWER COMMANDS TO KEEP HANDY

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Better first draft | Role + goal + constraints before you start |
| Find weaknesses | "Where is this weak? What's missing?" |
| Protect what's working | "Keep [X]. Change only [Y]." |
| Get unstuck | "Give me 3 versions — make them genuinely different" |
| Force structure first | "Before you write, tell me your plan" |
| Challenge your thinking | "Steel-man the opposite position" |
| Cut without killing | "Cut by half without losing the soul" |
| Expose assumptions | "What are you assuming here?" |
